items.text: The hub now publishes the live announcements as a plain list at its announcements.json address, for every app or for one app only. The other HOP apps can show them on their dashboards. Reason: announcements were typed in one place but no app could read them.

The dashboard now shows one announcement card, like the other apps: an urgent one first, otherwise the newest. A normal announcement can be hidden for a week with the Hide button, an urgent one cannot, and a link leads to the full list when there are more. Reason: up to three cards at once made the page busy.

The public announcements list and each announcement page now follow your language in all nine languages, including the dates and app names. The text of an announcement stays in the language it was written in. Reason: the page labels were always English.

The foot of the sidebar is now a short list going down: Help, Terms, Privacy, Changelog, GitHub and Announcement, then a line saying the hub is part of Hop Easy Link. It scrolls together with the menu, so it can be reached on a short screen and in the phone menu. Reason: the same foot is now used in every HOP dashboard, and the hub had only two links.
The Delete account button now opens the delete section of Settings directly. Reason: it used to leave you at the top of the Account tab.

An app can now ask the hub for a sign-in that is recent before it lets you do something sensitive. If your last sign-in is older than the app asks for, the hub shows the sign-in page once more, with the note that it needs to confirm it is you, and takes you straight back to the app after you sign in. Reason: until now an app could not tell a sign-in from a minute ago from a browser left open for weeks. The sign-in time is only counted when you really sign in with a password, with Google, by signing up, or with the code of two-factor sign-in, never when the browser remembers you, and only this browser is signed out, not your other devices.

The delete section now has its own link, so an app can send you straight to it: opening it shows the Account tab and scrolls down to Delete account. Reason: the apps said where to delete the account but could only point at the top of the page.

The warning now names every app whose data goes with the HOP ID: LinkHop, BioHop, PixelHop, NoteHop, FileHop and PayHop, in all nine languages. Reason: the old text listed only some kinds of data and left out FileHop and PayHop.

Revoking or creating an API token, or entering a wrong value in that form, now leaves you on the API tokens tab with the result message, instead of throwing you back to the Account tab. Reported after a hand test: the page reloaded without remembering the tab.

A wrong password when turning two-factor on or off, or when renewing recovery codes, now keeps you on the two-factor tab and shows the message there. The same rule as for tokens was missing in these forms.
Changing the language while on another tab of Settings no longer jumps to the Account tab, because the tab now stays in the address.
When scripts are blocked, a newly made token is now shown once on the page. Before, the token was made but never displayed, so it could not be copied.

For a signed-in person, the logo and the Back link on the announcements, status and changelog pages, the app list in the top bar and the Open buttons now lead to the dashboard instead of the public home page. Visitors who are not signed in still go to the public home page. Reason: members found themselves on the public site when they only wanted to go back.

The Open button on the PayHop card now starts at PayHop's own dashboard, as it does for the other apps, instead of its public start page. Reason: signing in through the launcher should end where your work is.

On the page-not-found and the something-went-wrong pages, the button back now says "Back to your dashboard" and leads there when you are signed in, and keeps leading to the home page when you are not. Reason: signed-in people were sent to the public home page after a wrong address.

The web framework the hub runs on was updated to a version that fixes a reported weakness in how background tasks report their output. Reason: the dependency audit had started to flag the old version.

The page now shows one card per release of each app, with a short title and a list of what changed, where, what it means for you and why, instead of a stream of commit and pull request titles. The text of the entries stays in English; the page labels are in all nine languages. Reason: the old list was hard to read and showed internal wording.
Every earlier release of the hub was rewritten in the same plain form.

Pages that follow the chosen language (home, about, privacy and the other information pages) now tell shared caches that the answer depends on the language cookie. Effect: a visitor no longer receives a page in somebody else's language from a cache. Files and the public numbers are unchanged, and signed-in pages are still never stored.

A visit without a language cookie no longer receives clean-up cookies, so a plain page answer carries no HOP cookie at all. Choosing a language with the language link sets only the one cookie for all HOP sites. A browser that still holds the old cookie is cleaned up once, as before.

entries.title: One theme and one language for the whole family

items.text: The page no longer claims that one token works at every HOP API. Hub tokens are for LinkHop; the form offers only what LinkHop accepts, and PixelHop, which has its own keys, is listed separately with where to make them and read about them. A new token can no longer carry a PixelHop permission; a token that already does keeps working. Reason: people tried hub tokens at PixelHop and got refused. Shown in all nine languages.

The light or dark choice and the language are now one choice for the whole family: set it on hel.ink and it holds on hub.hel.ink and the other way round, and the page is drawn in the right theme from the first moment. An old saved choice is moved over once. Reason: choices made in one HOP app were not followed in the next.
A library used for encryption was updated to fix a reported weakness that let a crafted key use up processor time. The security audit of dependencies is clean again.
New automatic checks cover the token form, the API page, the cookie rules and the first-paint theme script, so these behaviours do not break again unnoticed.

entries.title: Faster sign-in and sign-out, safer accounts

items.text: Signing in no longer waits for outside services. The login is recorded at once and the place and proxy lookups for the history are done in the background, so a slow lookup cannot hold you up. Until then a new history row shows no place. Reason: a slow or unreachable lookup service made sign-in slow.

Signing out no longer walks your browser through every app. The hub tells the apps to end your session in the background; an app's session ends within a second or two. Reason: the chain of redirects was slow and could stop halfway when one app was down. If the background delivery fails, the apps notice within five minutes.
An event that cannot be delivered to an app after all retries is now counted and shown to the administrators, without any personal data. Reason: failed deliveries used to go unnoticed.

Throwaway e-mail addresses are refused wherever an address is set: sign-up, changing your e-mail address and a new Google sign-up. Existing accounts are not touched. Reason: many fake accounts came from such addresses.

Imperium can now create, edit, publish, unpublish and delete announcements through the hub, and shows each account's API tokens (never their values) and ten recent logins. Reason: announcements could only be managed on the hub's own old pages.

Suspending an account, deleting it or changing its roles now needs a named administrator, an administrator cannot suspend or delete their own account, and only an owner can change roles. Reason: these actions must always be traceable to a person.
An account that is already linked to a Google account signs in to that account only, and no sign-in can move a Google link from one account to another.

items.where: Accounts that never verified their e-mail
items.text: When Google proves the address of such an account, the password of the earlier sign-up is replaced and its sessions, tokens and two-factor settings are removed, so nobody who registered an address first can keep access. A reset of the password by e-mail does the same. Reason: someone could register another person's address before they did.

Changing your e-mail address needs your current password, tells the old address and ends your other sessions. Changing your password, turning two-factor off or setting a password after a Google sign-up also ends your other sessions. The session you are using stays. In the apps you may have to sign in again once.
Suspending now also ends the account's sessions in the hub and in the apps at once, and removes its API tokens.
The notice about an e-mail change is in the account's language and shows the new address only in part.

PayHop (pay.hel.ink) is the seventh HOP app. It has its own page, its card on the home page and dashboard, entries in the FAQ, help, privacy and terms texts, and appears in the family menus, in all nine languages. Its dashboard card shows no numbers because it only keeps payment methods for people who choose to save them.
A new version of the terms (2026-11-11) names FileHop and PayHop. It is not required of anyone yet; the earlier text is unchanged.
The command to turn off two-factor for an account that lost its authenticator is now official, so support has a safe way back in for people who lost access. It leaves a record without any secret.
Accounts with a role get an Open Imperium button in the top bar, in nine languages.
Apps can ask the hub whether you are still signed in without showing any page. Reason: apps need to notice a sign-out elsewhere without interrupting you.
The hub now serves its site map, which answered not found before, so search engines can list the pages.
The picture of how one account serves every app is now a globe you can turn, with each app on its surface. Without scripts or with reduced motion the flat version is shown as before.
The small numbered labels are gone, and the text no longer says how many apps there are, so adding an app does not make it wrong.

Cards and panels have a clearer outline in light and dark, the app cards sit in equal columns, and the gaps are even. The Open button on the FileHop card goes to the FileHop dashboard instead of its public page. The FileHop card shows its numbers so it is as tall as the others.

The hub no longer offers an Admin section: signing in always leads to the dashboard, and accounts with a role get one shortcut to Imperium. Reason: the hub is for people and Imperium for administrators.

The owner account may now turn on two-factor, confirm it and renew its recovery codes for itself, because Imperium refuses an account without it. Turning it off stays blocked, and nobody else can touch the owner's two-factor.

The hop-assets logos and visuals were refreshed for all apps (a new look for the LinkHop and BioHop marks, one logo without text per app, each app name in its own typeface, scenes that finish drawing on the home page, and a more even layout of the boxes on the information pages). Reason: the family looked uneven.
The documentation site and the READMEs list seven apps in nine languages, and the install guides cover PayHop and FileHop.
The last 24 hours of failures show one row per app with a dot, the count, the time of the last failure and a small strip of the day, and a calm message when there is none.

The hub can send you back to the app you left after signing out, but only to an address that belongs to a HOP app; anything else leads to the hub home. Reason: signing out of an app used to end on the hub home page.
The HOP strip is the first row, the language row is gone from the footer (the language menu is in the top bar), and the copyright line is right-aligned on desktop and centred on phones.
The history had stopped at 4 November because it was built from stale data; it was rebuilt and a check now fails when it falls behind.

entries.title: Shared dialogs and a cleaner dashboard

items.text: Questions and warnings now appear as one shared HOP dialog in every app instead of the browser's own boxes, with a red button that names what will be deleted, keyboard use first and no motion under reduced motion. Reason: the browser boxes looked different everywhere and could be blocked.
Reminder cards on the dashboard can be hidden for a week.
A guide lists every place to change when a new app joins the family.
The FAQ, help, contact, about, app pages and status texts that were still shown in English now appear in every language.

Buttons, inputs and menus follow one shape and size across the dashboard, Settings, sign-in and administration pages, with text of 16 px and touch targets of 44 px on phones. Reason: controls looked different from page to page and were small on phones.
A calmer, flat look is available as an optional Clean style in Settings; the HOP look stays the default.
The top bar title and the Deleted badge are translated, links that open a new tab show an arrow, the logo opens the HOP ID dashboard and the sidebar lists the HOP family.

FileHop gets its own pixel logo and amber colours, appears in the home page diagram (it was missing), and is named in the privacy, terms and FAQ texts. The languages answer in the FAQ now lists the nine languages (it named eight, including Arabic).
The shortcuts to the security, data and tokens tabs open the tab they name, and on phones the active tab is scrolled into view.
The hub reports LinkHop's abilities from its own record instead of a fixed list.
Hand-offs from an app are no longer counted as real sign-ins.
Starting Google sign-in while no terms are required failed with an error; it now works.
It names the real addresses and documentation of LinkHop and PixelHop and no longer links pages that do not exist at BioHop and NoteHop.
The status page answers while the database is down, with no numbers, as the home page already did.
It follows the visitor's language and speaks of HOP, not LinkHop.
The expired-page, too-many-requests and not-found notices follow the chosen language.
Forged values sent as lists in the address or forms now count as missing instead of causing an error page.
A photo above 50 megapixels is refused before it is opened, and uploads are limited to 20 a minute.

entries.title: First stable release
entries.summary: The first stable release of the hub. Everything below existed before and from now on later releases build on it.

items.text: One account for LinkHop, BioHop, PixelHop and NoteHop, with sign-up and sign-in by e-mail or Google, e-mail verification, password reset, two-factor with recovery codes, a bot check, a profile with a photo and API tokens.
Signing in at the hub signs you in to the apps, and signing out at the hub signs you out of them. The secrets that protect this can be changed without downtime.

The hub tells each app when a profile changes, an account is suspended, restored or deleted, or sessions end. Deliveries are signed and retried. Reason: apps must follow the account without asking you again.
A signed interface lets the administration app see accounts, statistics and logs and act on accounts. Owner accounts and the configured main administrator are protected from these actions.
A home page that tells the story of the family, one page per app, terms, privacy, FAQ, help, about, a status page that checks every app, live numbers from the project page, and a history page.
A launcher for the family, a card with numbers per app, and the same frame as the apps: a sidebar with the HOP family and a top bar with the main action, language, theme and account.
Logos, fonts and the home page engine are served from the hub in fixed versions so every app looks the same.
The interface, READMEs and documentation site are in English, Chinese, German, Indonesian, Japanese, Portuguese, Spanish, French and Russian. Arabic and right-to-left layout were removed.
Install and update scripts, a documentation site and a security policy let others run their own copy.
New accounts can be asked to accept a versioned set of terms; it is off until the owner turns it on.
They are never stored by the browser, so Back after signing out does not show them again.
The pages after sign-up need a signed-in account, recovery codes are compared strictly, return addresses are checked, and the public status data carries only public fields.
Sign-in history and activity records are deleted after 90 days; backup copies are kept for 14 days on the same server, and the privacy page says so in all nine languages.
It also removes the data the apps hold, and the hub checks that each app did.
Links to encrypted NoteHop notes (the key is in the part after the hash sign) are refused, and pages are fetched only from the addresses that were checked.
They come from the hub's own host, and flags are country codes, not pictures from another site.
Error pages follow the visitor's language and the language cookie works when sessions are shared between hosts.
